records.name: Dagestan
records.current_summary: Dagestan falls within the North Caucasus regional exception identified by the UK Home Office CPIN (June 2025) and named in Canadian and Australian travel advisories as part of a distinct don't-travel zone. Canada specifically warns that visitors must obtain special permission from the Ministry of the Interior to enter certain areas. North Caucasus SOS's David Isteev states flatly that "there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus, and even private existence can trigger violence, detention, or forced return to families," adding that "every year it gets worse."  No separate Dagestan-specific written law or documented Chechnya-style purge exists, but the republic shares the same security-and-custom enforcement logic: the federal transition ban and propaganda law operate in a context where local security structures and family honour norms produce extrajudicial responses unmediated by legal process, and where special-access restrictions impede independent monitoring. This places Dagestan approximately 0.08 below the national score of 0.12. Well below the oblasts of central Russia (which sit at national) due to the regional-exception designation; above Chechnya (0.01), whose documented secret-prison and killing infrastructure has no confirmed equivalent in Dagestan.

sources.claim: UK Home Office Country Policy and Information Note on sexual orientation and gender identity/expression (June 2025): LGBT+ people, including in Chechnya, form a particular social group; there is generally no real risk of state persecution elsewhere in Russia from sexual orientation alone, but people in the North Caucasus, trans people, and public LGBT+ advocates are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution; between 2017 and 2024 Chechen and North Caucasus authorities carried out systematic campaigns against LGBT+ people including abductions, torture and extrajudicial killings, and violence in detention spread beyond the Caucasus after the 2023 'extremist' designation.

Government of Canada travel advisory for Russia: avoid all travel nationally; terrorist attacks are frequent in the republics of Chechnya, Dagestan and Ingushetia and the neighbouring Stavropol region; visitors must obtain special permission from the Ministry of the Interior to enter certain areas; elevated tensions flagged in the border regions with Georgia, including Kabardino-Balkaria (Mount Elbrus area).

Interview with North Caucasus SOS rights defender David Isteev ('Every year it gets worse'): there is 'no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus, and even private existence can trigger violence, detention, or forced return to families', worsening year on year.

records.name: Ingushetia
records.current_summary: Ingushetia is one of the republics explicitly named in the Canadian travel advisory's special-permission requirement (alongside Chechnya and Dagestan) and falls within the North Caucasus zone that the UK Home Office CPIN (June 2025) identifies as the exception to its finding of no state-persecution risk in Russia generally. Isteev of North Caucasus SOS states there is "no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus," where private existence can trigger violence, detention, or forced return to families.  Like Dagestan, Ingushetia shares the security-and-custom enforcement logic without a documented Chechnya-scale purge infrastructure. The special-access regime limits independent monitoring. Score approximately 0.08 below national (0.12). Equal to Dagestan in evidence quality; well above Chechnya (0.01), which has confirmed secret prisons and extrajudicial killings absent here.

records.name: Kabardino-Balkaria
records.current_summary: Kabardino-Balkaria is named within the broader North Caucasus risk zone identified by the UK Home Office CPIN (June 2025) and Western travel advisories. North Caucasus SOS's assessment that there is "no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus" encompasses this republic. The local security-and-custom enforcement logic—where family honour norms and informal security structures can produce violence, detention, or forced return to families—applies, even absent a specific documented purge infrastructure.  Unlike Chechnya, Dagestan, and Ingushetia, no separate special-permission entry requirement is specifically named for Kabardino-Balkaria in the Canadian advisory, and no Chechnya-scale extrajudicial detention site has been documented here. The deviation from national (0.12) is approximately 0.07 below. Slightly above Dagestan/Ingushetia (0.04) to reflect the absence of the explicit special-access regime; well below the central-Russian oblasts, which sit at national.

records.name: Karachay-Cherkessia
records.current_summary: Karachay-Cherkessia falls within the North Caucasus regional exception identified by the UK Home Office CPIN (June 2025) and named in Western don't-travel guidance for the Caucasus zone. The North Caucasus SOS assessment of no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the region applies here. The security-and-custom enforcement logic—informal detention, family exposure, violence unmediated by legal process—is the operative risk for a discovered visitor.  No Chechnya-style documented purge infrastructure or specific special-permission entry regime is identified for Karachay-Cherkessia. Approximately 0.07 below the national score of 0.12. Equal to Kabardino-Balkaria and North Ossetia in the broader North Caucasus bloc; above Dagestan and Ingushetia (0.04), which carry the explicit special-access designation.

records.name: Moscow
records.current_summary: Moscow concentrates enforcement activity of the federal anti-LGBT framework: club raids, the arrest of Kotov as the first person charged with *creating* an extremist organisation on LGBT grounds (late December 2024), and the medical and bureaucratic gatekeeping that the 2023 federal transition ban imposes. The Moscow Times' 2025 survey of persecution is titled around "arrests, club raids and extremism charges." A foreign visitor encountering Moscow police faces the federal propaganda-law penalty—up to 15 days' detention and deportation—applied in a jurisdiction with the highest police density and most active venue-level enforcement in the country.  The deviation from national (0.12) is approximately 0.03 below. The severity of the law is identical everywhere (it is federal), but Moscow's role as the primary venue for enforcement operations and its concentration of bureaucratic touchpoints (document verification, medical access, hotel registration) materially raise a visitor's probability of encountering active application. Comparable to Orenburg Oblast (0.09), which produced the country's first criminal extremism conviction against a commercial venue; both represent enforcement-active jurisdictions within the uniform federal framework.

records.name: NCR
records.current_summary: NCR carries the strongest protective legal framework in the Philippines: Quezon City enacted SP-3417, S-2025, a comprehensive SOGIESC anti-discrimination ordinance, and in July 2025 became the first LGU in the country to enact a Gender-Inclusive Health Ordinance creating a framework for gender-affirming primary care and specialised services. For a visitor, these represent the only enforceable protections in a country with no national anti-discrimination statute covering gender identity—complaint routes to a city health office or the QC Gender Desk that simply do not exist elsewhere.  Against that, two of the six documented killings of trans women in the 2024–2025 national series occurred here (Shaina Bayabay strangled in Pasig, March 2024; "Christine" stabbed in Valenzuela, September 2025), and EARIST state college reportedly denied enrollment to trans women requiring short haircuts (March 2024 video). The Commission on Human Rights issued public statements condemning both the campus practice and the killings, and arrests followed in Valenzuela.  Net effect: +0.09 above the national score. The ordinance belt gives a discovered visitor tangible institutional recourse unavailable in sibling regions; the violence, while real, is matched by arrests and official condemnation rather than impunity. Compare Soccsksargen (0.44), where a targeted activist assassination drew the CHR's own "cruelty and impunity" language without comparable protective infrastructure.

records.name: Soccsksargen
records.current_summary: Soccsksargen is the site of the record's most severe trans-related violence finding: on 23 June 2025 in General Santos City, a hooded gunman shot Ali Jejhon Macalintal, a transgender rights activist and radio commentator, several times at the acupuncture clinic she owned and fled on a motorcycle; police said they were investigating whether her history of activism was connected to the killing. Human Rights Watch called it an "apparent targeted killing". The national Commission on Human Rights publicly condemned the killings of two transgender women as "marked by cruelty and impunity" — an official body using the word impunity, the most damning official response language in the national record.  No protective ordinance, institutional counterweight or arrest in this killing is documented; the unresolved case is counted within the national series of six killings with arrests in at least three of them, none reported prosecuted to conviction.

records.name: Calabarzon
records.current_summary: In August 2025 in Lipa City, Batangas, Jericho Elliorante, 25, newly crowned winner of an LGBTQ pageant in Barangay Sambat, Tanauan City, was found dead with 13 stab wounds. Police opened a homicide case within days of the crowning — a faster institutional response than the unresolved General Santos shooting of the activist in Soccsksargen — but the killing is one of six in the 2024-2025 national series, and the 13-wound severity and LGBTQ-pageant context mark it as trans-implicated violence. The region has no protective ordinance cluster documented.

records.name: ARMM
records.current_summary: ARMM (predecessor to BARMM) is the only unit where a structurally different legal system applies to a visitor in conflict situations. The Bangsamoro Administrative Code (BAA-13, 2019) provides that justice in the autonomous region shall be dispensed "in consonance with the Constitution, Shari'ah, traditional or tribal laws." Parliament Bill No. 473 (July 2026) proposes a comprehensive Bangsamoro Shari'ah Justice System Code adding ta'zir criminal offences—the category under which morality offences against same-sex conduct and gender expression are prosecuted in comparable systems. Nationally, the Shari'ah court system is expanding: President Marcos Jr. signed a law in August 2024 creating three new Shari'ah judicial districts beyond BARMM, RA 12304 (September 2025) ensures equitable access, and the Supreme Court resolved in January 2026 to operationalise the Shari'ah High Court.  The dossier's assessor caveat is explicit: no source establishes that Philippine Shari'ah courts currently prosecute same-sex conduct or gender expression, and the original P.D. 1083 codified only personal law. The finding is structural—a jurisdiction with an active legislative process to create criminal religious law, in a region where a visitor's dispute may be adjudicated outside the Philippine court system entirely—rather than a documented enforcement reality.  Net effect: −0.07 below the national score. The risk is forward-looking and legal-framework-based, not enforcement-based, which limits the deviation under the "enforcement > statute" rule. However, the ta'zir drafting is the single most severe structural threat identified in the dossier for a transgender visitor, and the absence of any protective ordinance or civil-rights infrastructure in ARMM means no counterweight exists. Compare CAR (0.54), which also has a legal-pluralism concern but no criminal-law component.

records.name: CAR
records.current_summary: The Kalinga bodong/pagta system—bilateral inter-tribal peace pacts with their own holders, sanctions and dispute-resolution authority over "crimes and tribal-related offences"—was formally codified by the Kalinga provincial government in February 2026 as a 137-page written Pagta. Philippine courts recognise the bodong; academic literature frames it as legal pluralism in which indigenous and formal criminal justice coexist, with police handling customary-law cases. For a visitor whose dispute falls under a bodong's jurisdiction, the applicable institution may not be a Philippine court.  No trans-specific bodong ruling, customary exclusion, or gender-expression punishment was documented in the dossier. The constitutional recognition of indigenous justice also appears in the Bangsamoro Basic Law's IP-rights section, reinforcing the framework.  Net effect: −0.02 below the national score. The finding is a structural uncertainty (which court applies to you) without any evidence of trans-specific adverse outcome. It sits at the threshold of the minimum deviation. Compare ARMM (0.49), where the legal-pluralism concern is paired with an active criminal-law drafting process (ta'zir offences) that raises the stakes materially; here the bodong is a civil/ADR institution with no criminal-law expansion documented for morality offences.
